Show HN: I built a tool that finds reliability bugs in your code
items.summary: Hey HN, I’m Abhishek. I'm building Opslane, a tool that finds reliability issues in your code. On every PR, it spins up your entire app and then tries to find weak spots that would break in production. Demo: https://youtu.be/47phxkdh6f0 Example: We tested Opslane on Lago (open-source billing) and found a bug where customers get double charged. Opslane made Stripe take the money and then return a 500. Lago marked the payment failed. A retry from the dashboard charged the customer again. https://github.com/getlago/lago-api/issues/6903 Why I built this I used to work on reliability at Robinhood. We used to run chaos testing in our staging environments: inject faults in various parts of the system and see what breaks. We found issues like Kafka or Redis being unavailable for a few seconds could take the whole app down. But that kind of testing was expensive. It needed a well maintained staging environment. Engineers needed to know what to test. Most teams never actually did it. Over the last year, coding agents have gone writing some of my code to almost all my code now. Teams are shipping way more code than they were 6 months ago. Code review tools read the diff, but a lot of reliability bugs aren't in the diff. They're in how your code behaves when Stripe, Redis or the network misbehaves. And e2e tests usually mock those services out and test the happy path. Agents have made this type of testing a lot cheaper. And we will see more of this (kinda like security scanning / testing) How it works A full copy of your app per PR: Postgres, Redis, Kafka, SQS, S3. Working copies of your third-party dependencies: Stripe, Slack, Gmail and more. Traffic goes through our proxy, which lets us inject failures. The agent picks what to test: It reads every PR and writes down invariants that need to hold (for e.g. a customer should never be charged twice). It then injects faults likely to break the invariants. Bugs we've found We ran Opslane on some popular open-source apps and here are some of the bugs we have found: 1/ Twenty: deleting a workspace while Stripe is failing locks everyone out, and billing keeps going. Twenty merged a fix. ( https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/issues/28043 ) 2/ Dub: a restart in the middle of a payout paid a partner $240 for $120 owed. ( https://github.com/dubinc/dub.link/issues/4707 ) Full list: opslane.com/open-source Opslane is pretty early - we have a couple of early customers. We have found bugs in their system that their other code review tools missed. Would love to get feedback from folks and how they are seeing the reliability of their systems evolve over time with agents.

Show HN: OpenTaxRate – open-source US sales tax rates by street address
items.summary: I built this because I tried many sales tax APIs and the problems were: a) the rates were a black box with no source attached b) lookups resolved by ZIP code. ZIP codes are postal routes, not tax jurisdictions. Stripe's Tax team wrote a good post on this [1]: two houses in Drexel, MO share a city, a ZIP, and nearly a house number, but sit in different counties with different rates. If your lookup key is the ZIP, you are wrong on those addresses, even when the rate table is accurate. OpenTaxRate resolves the street address instead: - SST member states (24): the quarterly rate + boundary files, street ranges and ZIP+4, not just the rate tables - Non-SST states: a custom adapter for each state, using its DOR's own published tables and boundary files (TX Comptroller, FL DR-15DSS, ALDOR, IDOR, NY Pub 718, California via CDTFA's lookup, etc) - Census TIGER for geometry I tried with multiple open source geocoders you can self-host: Nominatim, Photon and Pelias, as well as proprietary ones (HERE, Geocodio, Mapbox, Google). Proprietary ones have higher accuracy, ~99.3% correct vs. 97.1% with just open source. For comparison: Avalara AvaTax 99.6%, TaxJar 98.2%. Public benchmark set are in the repo and at opentaxrate.com/benchmarks. Rates are just one part of sales tax, but also there's a ton of work in maintaining it as rules change. It doesn't handle exemptions, holidays, and caps. It returns the rate, plus the state's own location and jurisdiction codes for the address, resolved to the address, with its official source attached. MIT licensed, you can self-host with Postgres + PostGIS. [1]: https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-jurisdiction-resolut...

Show HN: Vu – a new programming language designed for AI. Rust speeds, Py syntax
items.summary: hi everyone! I wanted to share what I've been working on these past 6~ years. TL;DR: Rust is great, but somewhere along the way, I learned that I was too dumb to read and write Rust. As I worked on larger and larger Rust projects, I also became frustrated with the developer experience of working in Rust (slow compile time), so I wanted a better way. Vu's language changed a bit over time but the core principles remained the same: 1. It should be easy to read and write 2. It should be memory safe 3. It should be fast to run 4. It should be fast to compile Here's how I approached each: 1. Vu is syntactically very close to Python. The ownership rules are the ones Rust has, but I personally find it a lot easier to parse and understand. I've tested this with various LLMs and found it can read and write Vu out the box because of the similarity to Python. 2. Vu uses the same principles of Rust. Every value has one owner, borrows can't escape or outlive what they borrow, and nothing changes while it's borrowed. 3. Vu compiles down to C at the end of the day, so everything runs approximately at C speeds. 4. vuc check on the compiler’s own source (about 21,500 lines of Vu), takes about 0.4~ s. This check covers parsing, type and borrow checking. cargo check on a Rust project that size usually takes several seconds from scratch. Then there are other opinionated language decisions. Vu has no macros, Vu's borrow checker is lighter weight than Rust's with simpler interfaces and generics. However, in the past few years, as Vu's language evolved and AI began to take over, I expanded Vu's principles to include a couple additional principles: 5. It should be secure 6. It should be efficient for LLMs to write 5. I want to pen test Vu in public. In https://github.com/vu0tran/vu/tree/main/tests , you'll see a battery of tests where I'm trying to basically pwn Vu. There are explicit language decisions in there as well that tries to prevent a host of security flaws that exist in other languages, e.g, integer overflow stops the program instead of quietly wrapping around. 6. The syntax of Vu is designed to be tokenizer efficient. In addition, when Vu checks throws errors, the errors are designed to be token efficient and written in a way that guides LLMs to more easily fix bugs, reducing turns overall. So, in summary, Vu is still experimental. The compiler is 21,500 lines of Vu and compiles itself. The standard library also has TLS, HTTP/2, WebSockets and a PostgreSQL client, all tested against Python’s implementations and hostile input. I think most of the pieces are there. It does also compile down also to WebAssembly so you can play around w/ the checker on the website! Feel free to try to break it! What's next: 1. Figure out how to get Vu to perform faster than Rust 2. Rewrite some OSS libraries in Vu to further prove the language

items.title: A garbage collector for LLM context windows, written in Rust
items.summary: Hi HN, Like many of you, I spend a lot of time coding with Codex and switching between cloud and local models. As a software engineer, something I never understood, and honestly hated—was `/compact` and the way it’s designed. On local models my GPU screams, and after a few hours prefill takes 2 to 3 minutes per turn. On cloud models, as the context grows, the model starts getting noticeably dumber. IMHO the root problem is context bloat and the fact that compaction destroys the quality of the model's working memory. Looking under the hood and studying how attention works, I learned that memory in modern harnesses is basically "append-only." and attention on long context becames less effective due to the attenttion dead zone. So you end up having in the context thousands of lines of old compiler dumps and duplicate file reads sitting there rent free destroying the agent's attention. Having an LLM write a summary of your conversation and blowing away your KV-cache makes no engineering sense imho especially on local models where prompt prefill latency is critical (and on cloud models where you lose prompt-cache discounts). So I built a piece of software called *contextWatcher* (or *`cw`* for friends and family). It’s a Rust proxy that runs locally on CPU ( in less than 2ms), and gives: 1. Shadow-Deduplication: Computes BLAKE3 hashes of file reads. If the agent reads for example a file like `src/main.rs` at Turn 2, edits it at Turn 5, and reads it again at Turn 9, Turns 2 and 5 are replaced with 1-line pointer stubs. Only the latest version stays in context. 2. Surgical Tool Pruning: Truncates runaway compiler output (keeping the tool_call_id, invocation, and the panic/exit trace intact) so schemas and error context never break. 3. Tail Rule Pinning: Dynamically mirrors critical system constraints (from AGENTS.md) right above the latest user prompt, pulling them out of the middle attention dead-zone without invalidating the cached prefix. 4. Swarm Prefix Multiplexing: When multiple subagents collaborate on the same workspace, cw extracts the shared root prefix (tools, rules, system prompt) so local inference engines (llama.cpp / vLLM) only keep one copy in VRAM. 5. Cache Preservation: Operates without rewriting the stable prefix, keeping prompt caching intact. On my local dual AMD GPU (Radeon Instinct Mi50 32GB) setup with a ~28k context session, cleaning out this dead weight dropped prompt prefill from ~170 seconds down to ~1.6 seconds and unlike fuzzy compaction, ground-truth code stayed 100% intact and all unit tests passed. It's open source (MIT / Apache-2.0) and installs via a one-liner: ```curl -fsSL https://constant-labs.com/cw-install.sh | sh``` Repo: https://github.com/GionaGranchelli/context-watcher For me and my setup worked pretty well, and I am satisfied with the result I get, I am really curious to see other people testing it and giving me an honest feedback on the tool and the approach

items.title: Show HN: Interview your analysts instead of auto-generating a semantic layer
items.summary: I’ve spent the last year building context for AI analysts in the mid-market. I’ve open sourced a library from my learnings, along the same principles of the Matt Pocock skills. Principles: * Claude / Codex / Cursor etc are great data agents - you just need context to enable them to answer business questions correctly. * Much of the important context lives in analysts heads' * Context must be maintainable (short, human readable - markdown and yaml) * Added context should be load bearing, not repeat of information that is available in another source of truth - and evaluations prove the value of the context * Companies should own their own context, and must be shareable with any model * Context should be version controlled (and github works as a context store). What the library does: * Performs an interview with your analysts (context-interview skill), one domain at a time, similar to what I have done as a consultant. The interview is informed by your query logs. * The AI develops evaluation questions at the same time as building the context - and at the end of each domain interview asks you to run an evaluation with and without the context. The evaluation will actually check the results against your dashboards if you allow it. We have shown increases in accuracy from 87% to 95% by adding this context in our imaginary open-source company, Shorelane. * Provides a set of skills to use the context that follow best practices for self service analytics: * Write a plain english plan for the business user to approve * Execute the plan * Verify that the execution followed the plan, and provide a simple uncertainty score. * Enable a adversarial review of the answer if their are doubts. What you get: Context repo written in markdown and yaml after you finish the interview. We use a single github repo, divided into domains. The interview can be shared and restarted by checking in/out of github. A set of skills to share with your business team Optional: We offer a fast MCP server to serve the Github-based context to your team.
